# Fan accelerates increasingly when idle/at a stop

Your 2004 Jeep Grand Cherokee exhibiting fan acceleration while idling, accompanied by temperature spikes above 210Â°F and audible clicking, points to a specific failure mode in the cooling control loop. The behavior where the system seems fine immediately after a restart but degrades as heat builds up indicates that the control logic is compensating for a lack of airflow rather than a simple electrical short.

In this era of automotive electronics, the engine cooling fan is rarely controlled by a single relay anymore. Instead, it operates under the command of a Powertrain Control Module (PCM), which receives inputs from the Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor and the Fan Speed Sensor (FSS). The PCM calculates the duty cycle required to maintain optimal operating temperature based on these inputs. When you hear the fan accelerating progressively while parked, the ECT sensor is likely reporting a value higher than the actual coolant temperature, or the PCM has detected insufficient airflow and is ramping up the fan speed in an aggressive attempt to shed heat.

The clicking noise you describe is a critical diagnostic clue. Most electronic fans use a three-wire configuration: power, ground, and a control signal. If the fan motor is failing open circuit, the PCM will detect this loss of load or lack of feedback from the FSS. In response, the ECU may attempt to re-energize the relay repeatedly or cycle the fan at maximum speed in short bursts, creating that distinct clicking sound as the relay engages and disengages rapidly. This is often a "limp mode" behavior where the system tries to prevent overheating despite the component failure.

To diagnose this effectively without immediately replacing expensive assemblies, you need to isolate whether the issue lies with the sensor data or the actuator itself. Start by verifying the resistance of the Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor. If the sensor is reading too hot due to a failed thermistor, the PCM will command the fan to run at high RPMs even when the engine is merely warm. This mimics an overheating condition and explains why the issue appears after sitting for a while; the coolant sits stagnant, and if the sensor is faulty, it might report a temperature that triggers maximum cooling duty immediately upon restart until the PCM re-evaluates the data.

If the ECT sensor checks out, the fault likely resides in the Fan Speed Sensor (FSS) or the fan motor assembly itself. The FSS provides feedback to the PCM regarding the fan's rotation speed. If this sensor is intermittent, the PCM might think the fan has stopped spinning and will aggressively drive it back up, causing the clicking as the relay tries to maintain communication. You can test this by visually inspecting the connector at the rear of the fan assembly for corrosion or loose pins.

Another possibility involves the cooling fan relay located in the Power Distribution Box under the hood. If the internal contacts are pitted or if the coil is failing, it may not provide a solid connection until the current draw increases significantly, leading to the erratic acceleration behavior. Swapping this relay with a known good unit from another vehicle of the same model year is a low-cost diagnostic step that can rule out actuator failure.

Replacing the entire fan assembly is often the most pragmatic solution if individual component testing yields inconclusive results. The integrated sensor and motor in the 2004 Grand Cherokee are designed as a single unit, making it difficult to swap just the motor or the sensor without risking damage to the wiring harness. Ensure that when you install the new assembly, you clear any stored fault codes in the PCM using an OBD-II scanner. Sometimes, even after replacing the hardware, the ECU retains a "history code" for fan system failure that prevents it from commanding the fan until a specific drive cycle is completed.

If you are dealing with similar thermal management issues in software-defined vehicles, the principles remain the same: the controller (ECU) relies on sensor fidelity to actuate the cooling system. In modern systems using Laravel or other frameworks for IoT vehicle diagnostics, you would implement a fallback mechanism where, if the FSS signal is lost, the system defaults to maximum fan speed rather than assuming normal operation, mirroring the safety logic your Jeep's PCM is currently attempting to enforce.

Ultimately, addressing the clicking noise and temperature spike requires verifying the integrity of the ECT sensor data, ensuring the Fan Speed Sensor is communicating correctly, and confirming the relay and fan motor assembly are capable of sustaining continuous load without intermittent failures.
